title: The Pointer That Was Right Yesterday: Invalidation, and Borrowing From Something That Moves

questions.question: You hold a pointer to samples.back(), then push_back one more reading. What happened to your pointer?
options: It may now refer to freed memory, because the vector may have moved its buffer to make room
Nothing: a vector keeps its elements in place and only the size changed
It now points at the new element
It is fine as long as you do not write through it
questions.explanation: Measured with three readings and no slack: capacity went from 3 to 6 and the buffer moved. Everything borrowed from the old buffer refers to memory that has been handed back, and nothing warns.

questions.question: Twenty push_backs into an empty vector caused how many reallocations, and why does that number matter?
options: Six, and it matters because the other fourteen insertions left every borrowed pointer valid, which is how the bug survives testing
Twenty, one per insertion, so the bug is easy to find
One, at the first insertion only
None, because vectors allocate their full capacity up front
questions.explanation: Capacities went 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32. Most insertions are harmless, which is exactly why a borrowed pointer passes a test suite and fails when a sample buffer gets one element longer.

questions.question: You reserve room, then erase an element from the middle. What happens to a pointer you saved to a later element?
options: It stays valid and points at a different reading, and no sanitizer reports anything
It dangles, and the address sanitizer reports a use after free
It is unaffected, because erase only changes the size
The vector reallocates, so it dangles
questions.explanation: Measured: the storage was identical and the address that held 30 then held 40. Nothing was freed, so there is no use after free to detect. A live pointer to the wrong reading is worse than a dangling one that crashes.

questions.question: Does storing an index instead of a pointer protect you from an erase?
options: No: an index into a vector is invalidated by an erase exactly as a pointer is, and for the same reason
Yes, that is the standard fix for all invalidation
Yes, as long as the index is below the erase point
Only if the vector was reserved first
questions.explanation: An index survives reallocation, which is E-MEM-0011, and not an erase, which shifts everything down. For an erase the answer is to look the element up by identity rather than by position.

questions.question: Why does same_storage compare the capacity as well as the address?
options: An allocator may hand a freed buffer straight back for the next request, so two different buffers can share an address
Because the address is not stable between runs
To make the comparison faster
Because data() returns null for an empty vector
questions.explanation: A vector that reallocated can land at the address it just released, which makes an address-only check report no change after every pointer it handed out was invalidated. Comparing capacity catches it, and predicting with would_reallocate avoids depending on allocator behaviour at all.

questions.question: Which of std::vector, std::deque and std::list moved their first element over 100 insertions?
options: Only the vector, and it is still the one to reach for first
All three, since all of them grow
None, since all three guarantee stable references
The deque and the list, because they allocate per element
questions.explanation: Measured: vector moved, deque and list did not. The other two buy element stability with a pointer chase per element, which phase 07 measures the cost of. Reserve a vector first, and reach for the others when you genuinely need stable addresses.
